name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 19 July 1977

clue.text: Concerning many meeting at Elaine's home

blocks.note: 'as to' means concerning or regarding
L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a crossword stand-in for many
taken as written

explanation.surface: A crowd gathering at the house of a woman named Elaine.
explanation.walkthrough: Elaine is the lily maid of Arthurian legend, whose home in Malory and Tennyson is ASTOLAT.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian romance Elaine is known as the Fair Maid of Astolat, the town where she lived.

clue.text: Name of character in Stalky & Co.

definitions.text: Name of character in Stalky & Co.

blocks.clueFragment: Name of character in Stalky & Co.
blocks.note: surface reading: one of the schoolboys or masters in Kipling's stories
setter's reading: a printed symbol, and the one in the title is the & sign

explanation.walkthrough: Stalky & Co. is Kipling's book of school stories, so the clue seems to want a pupil's name; the character meant is the typographic symbol in its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The ampersand is the name of the & symbol, standing for and.

clue.text: "Subjects' feet May hourly - on their sovereign's head" (Richard II)

definitions.text: "Subjects' feet May hourly - on their sovereign's head" (Richard II)

blocks.clueFragment: "Subjects' feet May hourly - on their sovereign's head"
blocks.note: a line from Shakespeare with its verb missing
the play: the deposed king imagines being buried where people walk over him

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation to complete: in Act III Richard pictures a grave in the highway, where subjects' feet may hourly tread on him.
explanation.definitionFit: To trample is to tread heavily on something, which the passing feet do to the buried king's head.

clue.text: Settles point connected with picture

blocks.note: a bird lands, or settles, on a branch
a cape is a point of land jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: Someone settles an argument point concerned with a painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' suggests an argument; it is a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape is a picture of a stretch of countryside.

clue.text: Little children in glasses?

definitions.note: a phrase for the noun: small measures of spirits, served in glasses

blocks.note: first meaning: toddlers
second meaning: small drinks of whisky or rum poured into glasses

explanation.walkthrough: Glasses suggests children wearing spectacles; they are drinking glasses holding small drams.
explanation.definitionFit: Tots are small children, and a tot is also a small drink of spirits.

clue.text: Cosmonaut uses silencer before Iran trip

indicators.note: to trip is to stumble, so the country's name falls out of its usual order

blocks.note: a gag silences someone
the country's four letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: A Soviet space traveller packs a muffler for a journey to Iran.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' reads as a journey to Iran; it is the signal to rearrange IRAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuri Gagarin was the Soviet pilot who in 1961 became the first human in space.

clue.text: Fighters appear pleased one's holding up the list

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom to the top
to hold something is to keep it inside your grip

blocks.note: glad means pleased
one is I, and 's is short for is
a rota is a list of duties

explanation.surface: Soldiers look pleased because someone is delaying the roster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding up the list' sounds like delaying it; it means I'S holds the list turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladiators were men who fought in Roman arenas, so they are fighters by trade.

clue.text: Note to plant to provide a vice

blocks.note: a note of the musical scale
a reed is a tall waterside grass

explanation.surface: Instructions to plant something in order to make a vice.
explanation.walkthrough: Greed, or avarice, is one of the seven deadly sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Greed is excessive desire for wealth or food, counted among the classic moral failings.

clue.text: Was a country backward in road-planning?

definitions.text: Was a country backward in road-planning?

blocks.note: surface reading: a former nation that lagged behind in building highways
setter's reading: a rural area whose lanes are full of grooves, named for its rutted land

explanation.walkthrough: Rutland was the smallest English county until it was merged in 1974, so it 'was' one; its name reads as rutted land, as if its roads were never improved.
explanation.definitionFit: Rutland was an English county abolished in 1974, the year before this clue's era, and restored in 1997.

clue.text: Annoys police informers

blocks.note: first meaning: a slang verb for irritates
second meaning: slang nouns for those who tell tales to the police

explanation.walkthrough: One word, verb then noun: British slang for irritates, and for informers.
explanation.definitionFit: To nark is to irritate in British slang, and a nark is a police spy or informer.

clue.text: Sea-food for man on board includes ray's head

indicators.note: one thing includes another by holding it inside itself
the head of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: a chessman, the humblest piece on the board
the first letter of ray

explanation.surface: A sailor's fish supper that has a bit of ray in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man on board' suggests a sailor; here the board is a chessboard and the man a PAWN, which takes R inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A prawn is a small shellfish eaten as seafood.

clue.text: Sycophant takes in owner of Grahame's Hall

blocks.note: Mr Toad owns Toad Hall in Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows
one who takes food in

explanation.surface: A flatterer welcomes the master of Toad Hall into his home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes in' looks like a signal to put one word inside another, but here it is a noun phrase in disguise: one who takes in food.
explanation.definitionFit: A toad-eater was originally a charlatan's assistant who pretended to eat toads; it came to mean a fawning flatterer, whence toady.

clue.text: Meal for Dad inter alios

indicators.note: inter is Latin for among or between, so one item sits inside the other

blocks.note: Latin for others; the others are the rest
an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A dinner laid on for father, among other people.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin tag 'inter alios' means among others; the setter splits it so that inter is the instruction and alios the others.
explanation.definitionFit: A repast is a formal word for a meal or the food served at one.

clue.text: The captain's revolver?

blocks.note: surface reading: the pistol a ship's master carries
setter's reading: something on deck that turns round, a winch for hauling the anchor

explanation.walkthrough: A revolver is a handgun, but here it is anything that revolves; on a ship that is the drum turned to raise the anchor.
explanation.definitionFit: A windlass is a horizontal winch, turned by a crank, used on ships to haul up the anchor cable.

clue.text: Thief in biggest High Street hold-up?

definitions.text: Thief in biggest High Street hold-up?

blocks.note: surface reading: a robber in a huge armed raid on the main shopping street
setter's reading: one who raises a whole store into the air, the shop itself

explanation.walkthrough: A hold-up is a robbery, but read literally the biggest high-street lift would be raising a whole store; the thief who does that takes from stores.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoplifter is a thief who steals goods from a store while pretending to be a customer.

clue.text: Region round the Pole as a battleground

indicators.note: one thing placed round another encloses it

blocks.note: a region is an area
N for the North Pole

explanation.surface: The Arctic regarded as a theatre of war.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a place of contest, literally the sanded floor where gladiators fought.

clue.text: Like a match struck by the impetuous

definitions.text: Like a match struck by the impetuous

blocks.note: setter's reading: a struck match has a burning tip
surface reading: a describing word for rash, impulsive people

explanation.walkthrough: Two descriptions of one adjective: a lit match literally has a fiery top, and rash people are said to be this.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot-headed means rash and quick to anger, and a lit match has a hot head.

clue.text: Run on occasion might decide the match

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the noun: the period that might decide it

blocks.note: in cricket a run not scored off the bat, such as a bye or wide, is an extra
an occasion is a time, as in 'that time'

explanation.surface: A single run scored at a key moment could settle a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an extra is a run credited to the batting side without being hit, such as a wide or a no-ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra time is the added period played when a match is level, which may produce the winner.

clue.text: Unsafe, as many a surgeon found out

indicators.note: found here is to cast or forge, and out adds disorder, so the letters are remade

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral 500, a crossword stand-in for many
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Many surgeons have discovered that a risky operation is risky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found out' reads as discovered; it is the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dangerous means likely to cause harm, the opposite of safe.

clue.text: Barker's affection for painting?

blocks.note: first meaning: a viral disease of dogs; an affection is an old word for an ailment
second meaning: a water-based paint, or painting done with it

explanation.surface: A dog's fondness for art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affection' looks like fondness but is the medical sense, a disease; a barker is a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Distemper is both a canine disease and a glue-bound paint used on walls and scenery.

clue.text: Keeping pay?

definitions.note: storage is a charge, so it stands for the fee rather than the act of paying

blocks.note: first meaning: the safe keeping of goods in a warehouse
second meaning: the fee charged for keeping them there

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as holding on to your wages; the two words are separate senses of one noun, the keeping of goods and the fee for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Storage is the keeping of goods in a place, and also the charge made for keeping them there.

clue.text: Italian city has one spell bound

indicators.note: something bound is held fast, here inside another word

blocks.note: a spell or stint, as in taking your turn
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A northern Italian city is under a magic enchantment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell bound' suggests enchantment; spell is a stint, TURN, which holds I.
explanation.definitionFit: Turin, Torino in Italian, is the capital of Piedmont in northern Italy.

clue.text: Push off with fifty rupees perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals the letters may stand in some other arrangement

blocks.note: Roman numeral fifty
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is told to clear off, handed fifty rupees.
explanation.definitionFit: To repulse is to drive back or repel an attack or an advance.

clue.text: Crop said to be newly scattered

blocks.clueFragment: Crop said to be newly scattered
blocks.note: surface reading: seed for a crop freshly broadcast over a field
setter's reading: the answer's Greek root is said to mean scattered like sown seed, so the word describes things dotted about

explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Greek sporas, scattered, from speirein, to sow, the same root as spore; the clue leans on that history.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occurring here and there or now and then, as if scattered at random.

clue.text: Green ties coming up

indicators.note: in a down entry coming up means read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a tie is a drawn game, so ties are draws

explanation.surface: Environmentally minded neckwear is becoming fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' and 'ties' suggest neckties; ties are drawn matches.
explanation.definitionFit: A sward is an expanse of short grass, a lawn or village green.

clue.text: Musketeer has a doubtful character, in short

indicators.note: in short means abbreviated, so the words are clipped

blocks.note: taken as written
though expresses doubt or reservation
taken as written

explanation.surface: One of Dumas's swordsmen is a shady figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are clipped as in speech: though becomes tho', and has becomes 's, giving A + THO' + 'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Athos is one of the three musketeers in Alexandre Dumas's novel, with Porthos and Aramis.

clue.text: Specimen obtained by politician in auction

indicators.note: one item placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: an auction is a sale
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician bids for a specimen at an auction house.
explanation.definitionFit: A sample is a small part taken as an example of the whole.

clue.text: Tax royalty on the old lines

blocks.note: first meaning: an old municipal levy
second meaning: a person of the line of the old Scottish crown

explanation.walkthrough: Scot is the old word for a tax, kept in the phrase scot-free; the second half points to a Scot, by way of the old Scottish royal line.
explanation.definitionFit: A scot was a medieval tax or payment, and a Scot is a native of Scotland, home of an ancient royal house.

clue.text: Indifferent, in a way, to call for retirement

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw or go back, so this word runs the other way

blocks.note: a way is a path, so 'a way' gives a path
to cite is to summon, as to court

explanation.surface: Someone unmoved by a summons to retire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call for retirement' reads as a retirement notice; call is CITE, and retirement turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Apathetic means showing no interest or concern, the same as indifferent.

clue.text: The dwelling is not all that big, look!

indicators.note: not all of the following words is used, only a stretch inside them

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a house is quite small after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not all that big' reads as modest size; it says only part of 'big, look' is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: An igloo is a domed Inuit dwelling built from blocks of snow.

clue.text: One's erred badly as a writer

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters are put in the wrong order

blocks.note: one is I, and 's is short for is
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone has made a mess of being an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore Dreiser was the American novelist who wrote Sister Carrie and An American Tragedy.

clue.text: Article pleads for return of old hero

indicators.note: on its return a word travels back the way it came

blocks.note: the definite article
one who sues pleads a case in court

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece calls for a former champion to come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' reads as a newspaper piece; it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: Theseus is the hero of Greek myth who killed the Minotaur in the Cretan labyrinth.
